    The Oberlin Review

    Unique New York! Wait, I Meant Oberlin.

    Sasha Bercovici, The Bulletin Editor • October 2, 2026
    Illustration by Theo Preston
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 8:50
    Instaread

    In many of my previous Bulletin articles, I treat Oberlin College and Conservatory as some special place. I leverage its historic reputation and cultural identity to examine or make a point about some aspect of Oberlin living. But this assumes that Oberlin is unique, which is something I have increasingly questioned in the past months.

    A lot of what I previously assumed was unique to Oberlin I now believe is attributed less to some ethereal quality of our College and more to the age group, cultural sphere, and status that we share as college students. Aren’t these same qualities shared among students across the nation? Among young, “artsy” adults across the globe?

    Going home for the summer, I was shocked to see how many strangers looked just like that Obie I see in Mudd every day — shocked how many times I squinted to see if that guy with an ironically cringe graphic tee and capri-jorts or that girl with brunette micro bangs and a plaid skirt was a friendly acquaintance from Oberlin, only to discover after their approach that they were simply a classic Los Angeles trust fund kid. The same happens when I visit my brother in Brooklyn.

    This is, of course, expected. LA and NYC schools are essentially Oberlin prep-factories at this point, but my Obie recognition goes farther. From the tiny Vashon Island in the Puget Sound to jazz bars in Bordeaux, France and Sofia, Bulgaria, I’ve met people my age obsessed with Marx, Godspeed You! Black Emperor, and thrifted clothes; typical “Obies.”

    Despite these experiences, however, Oberlin College is still the only higher-ed institution I’ve attended, making my viewpoint rather limited. For more informed perspectives, I reached out to transfer students, both to and from Oberlin, who have experienced a little bit of both worlds.

    Perhaps the biggest distinguishing factor between universities is academics. I chose Oberlin because I thought that classes here would focus on learning for its own sake instead of grades and career-chasing. So far, I have been perfectly satisfied with its mix of academic rigor and curiosity, but I wonder what it is like at different schools.

    For College third-year Indy DiGioia, classes at Oberlin have been a significant step up from his previous institution. DiGioia, who transferred from the University of Rhode Island this semester, praises Oberlin for its more niche classes and professorial quality.

    “Academically, [Oberlin is] definitely more rigorous and more organized,” DiGioia said. “The classes here themselves are much more interesting and niche, and you kind of need smart people to teach those. … I enjoy the professors a lot more, and they’re a lot more personable, and I’ve felt more connected to them.”

    DiGioia used his current class on pre-modern Indian history as an example, telling me that at URI, the same type of class wouldn’t exist.

    Violette Stevenson and Anna Steel, who both left Oberlin after their first year, see things differently. Stevenson, who now attends New York University Tisch School of the Arts, praises the school for its teaching style.

    “[At Oberlin] I did not find my classes very stimulating,” she said. “[At NYU] the work that I am receiving, in most cases, feels more thought out.” 

    Stevenson emphasized NYU’s focus on finding career and internship opportunities which are individually relevant for students.

    Steel, who now attends Columbia University, said both schools have “many great professors.” While she said she does have a heavier workload at Columbia, she speculated that it’s more because she was only taking intro classes at Oberlin back when she was a first-year.

    She makes a point. When using transfer students as our evidence, comparing the quality of schools is difficult. By the nature of transferring, the student will usually be comparing the rigor of upper-level courses at one school to lower-level courses at another.

    College second-year Jordan Ehrenberg’s testimony helps side-step this problem. Having transferred from Berklee College of Music last semester, Ehrenberg described stark differences between the intro-level audio engineering classes he took at both schools. Where Berklee’s class largely rehashed knowledge he learned in high school, the same class at Oberlin is consistently challenging.

    Taking all this into account, academic differences between Oberlin and other universities do exist in some capacity but are hard to define. Oberlin classes, while maintaining a similar workload to ultra-prestigious schools like Columbia and NYU, are perhaps less career-focused, instead emphasizing depth of learning about niche, if maybe impractical, subjects.

    While academics are important to our college, if Oberlin is unique on any front, I expect it to be its culture.

    The most obvious difference is the environment. Where social life here is defined by deeply interlinked small-town life, other schools find themselves right in the middle of bustling city life. Indeed, the search for an urban environment was a prime reason for Steel and Stevenson’s switch.

    “The Columbia social scene is more dispersed than Oberlin’s, in my experience,” Steel said. “Attending a large school in a large city means you know a smaller percentage of the people on campus, and everyone is headed somewhere different on a Friday night.” Stevenson also noted that NYU’s student body was more diverse.

    It is true that, at Oberlin, our proximity and small size lead to more of what Steel describes as “universal experiences” among the student body, which are impossible to have in schools that host tens of thousands of people. Stevenson, however, points out that despite NYU’s enormous size, her department, the Department of Photography and Imaging, is quite small, providing a similar sense of tight-knit community to that which she found at Oberlin.

    DiGioia, who attended a school not in the thicket of Manhattan skyscrapers but in the suburban sprawl of Rhode Island, notes walkability as one of Oberlin’s key qualities. He, a member of the Harkness House Co-op, also loves the diverse and collaborative community that Oberlin fosters, especially compared to the Greek Life dominating URI.

    “Here, people are way more [uniquely] individual,” he told me. “At my last school [there were] a lot of frats and sororities and conforming to the same way. … There’s a lot more range, taste, style, and different mediums of artistic expression [at Oberlin].” He went on to compare the different forms of organization found in Greek life and co-ops, describing fraternities as based on hierarchy while co-ops are based on mutual collaboration. More than anything, DiGioia highlights how Oberlin students create a welcoming environment for students of all backgrounds.

    For Ehrenberg, the key differences lie in the music scene. Despite Berklee being strictly a music school, he describes the bands there as more stilted, competitive, and just not his style.

    “I just came here, and I felt like I was immediately immersed,” he said. “There’s tons of great musicians here and tons of more interesting people here to play music. … I have a lot more opportunities and musical prospects here. It’s like I’ve only scratched the surface of it here.”

    Politically, where one would expect “woke-Mecca” Oberlin to shine like the North Star, most of those I interviewed noted the least difference. Ehrenberg and Stevenson described similar views in the student bodies of Oberlin and their other schools. Steel, while noting little difference in the views of professors, did note an increased percentage of conservative students at Columbia compared to Oberlin.

    DiGiaio noted the biggest changes: professors being less likely to speak out and conservative values imbued into the Greek life which dominated the school. He definitely feels more comfortable at Oberlin, where he describes people as more liberal and open-minded.

    Overall, it seems the differences people found between Oberlin and other colleges were often conflicting, changing from person to person and school to school. Oberlin certainly has distinguishing qualities: a small town environment, a de-emphasis on career-first education, and a thriving and diverse music scene. But other schools share these qualities as well. I’m sure you’re likely to find similar teaching styles in other liberal arts colleges; other colleges too share a small-town environment, and you will definitely find myriad musical circles in the city environments of NYU or Columbia.

    Additionally, transfer students are likely to choose a school radically different from the one they seek to leave; so while there are many differences between Oberlin and URI, for example, there might be fewer between Oberlin and Bard.

    But, while you are likely to find Obie-esque people in other worlds, or challenging courses at other schools, it seems to me that Oberlin is different in the way that it combines each of these specific characteristics into one school. Each other school mentioned has its own spread of defining qualities, some overlapping with Oberlin, some overlapping with each other. Oberlin is unique, but it is not alone in its uniqueness.
